name: Kosovo

facts.religion: Sunni Islam about 95%, Serbian Orthodox and Catholic minorities

snapshot: After repeated elections and deadlock, Kosovo finally chose a president in October 2026, weeks after a court convicted its wartime leader Hashim Thaçi.
culture: Kosovo's ethnic Albanian majority shares language and culture with Albania, while Serbian Orthodox monasteries, like Visoki Dečani, are sacred to Serbs. It has one of Europe's youngest populations. Athletes like judoka Majlinda Kelmendi, its first Olympic gold medallist, are national heroes.
society: Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008, nine years after a NATO bombing campaign ended a Serbian crackdown. About 100 countries recognise it; Serbia, Russia, China and five EU members do not. Remittances from the diaspora are vital. A Serb minority in the north resists Pristina's authority.
situation: In 1998-99, ethnic Albanian guerrillas of the Kosovo Liberation Army fought Serbian forces until NATO's bombing campaign forced Belgrade out. Kosovo declared independence in 2008; about 100 countries recognise it, but Serbia, Russia and China do not, and five EU states still refuse. Many Kosovars see the KLA's fighters as liberators. In 2026, an international court in The Hague called some of them war criminals, and Kosovo's politics nearly broke over it.

On 16 September, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, a court set up under Western pressure to try KLA crimes, convicted former president Hashim Thaçi and three other wartime leaders, sentencing them to a combined 81 years (Reuters via The Print). More than two weeks of protests followed, some violent, as people feared the verdict would tarnish the independence struggle (AP via ClickOnDetroit). At the same time, parliament faced a deadline: Kosovo's president needs a two-thirds vote, and failure in June had already forced one snap election. Just after midnight on 7 October, three minutes past the constitutional deadline, lawmakers elected economist Justina Shiroka Pula, head of the Academy of Sciences and Arts, with 81 votes, one more than required (European Western Balkans). The price of the deal between Prime Minister Albin Kurti's Vetëvendosje and the opposition PDK, Thaçi's old party, was a law limiting the Hague court's powers, which will anger the Western backers Kosovo depends on.
power: A parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the government with the support of the 120-seat Assembly, which includes 20 seats reserved for minorities; the president, elected by a two-thirds vote, is largely ceremonial but commands the armed forces and must sign laws.
holders: Prime Minister Albin Kurti (Vetëvendosje); President Justina Shiroka Pula, since 7 October 2026.
